name: Araunah
title: The Jebusite who owned the threshing floor on Moriah
summary: Aravna, who is called Ornan in the Chronicles books, was a Jebusite living in Jerusalem after David had conquered the city. He owned a threshing floor on Mount Moriah that became decisive in Israel's history. When a devastating plague struck the land as a result of David's census, the Lord's angel stopped at this threshing floor. At the prophet Gad's command, David went up to buy the place and build an altar. Aravna showed great generosity and offered to give the entire property with oxen and tools to the king without payment, but David firmly refused: he would not bring the Lord a sacrifice that had cost him nothing. This attitude expresses a fundamental biblical principle that true worship requires dedication and personal cost. David paid for the place, built the altar, and presented an offering, and the Lord stopped the plague. The site is identified in Jewish and Christian tradition with Mount Moriah, where Abraham was once willing to sacrifice Isaac. It later became the place where Solomon built the Lord's temple, thus linking Aravna's threshing floor together with the patriarchs' faith, the Davidic kingdom, and temple worship into one continuous line of salvation history.

keyEvents.title: The Plague over Israel
keyEvents.description: After David had sinned by conducting a census, God sent a plague upon Israel. The angel of the Lord stood at Araunah's threshing floor when the plague was stopped.

keyEvents.title: The Command of the Prophet Gad
keyEvents.description: The prophet Gad told David to go up to Araunah's threshing floor and build an altar to the Lord there, to stop the plague that had struck the people.

keyEvents.title: Araunah Offers the Threshing Floor for Free
keyEvents.description: When David came to buy the threshing floor, Araunah offered it along with oxen and tools to the king free of charge, but David refused to accept it without paying.

keyEvents.title: David Buys the Threshing Floor
keyEvents.description: David insisted on paying for the threshing floor because he did not want to offer to the Lord anything that cost him nothing. According to 2 Samuel, he paid fifty shekels of silver for the threshing floor and the oxen, while 1 Chronicles states six hundred shekels of gold, likely for the entire larger area that later became the temple site.

keyEvents.title: The Altar Is Built and the Offering Is Presented
keyEvents.description: David built an altar to the Lord on Araunah's threshing floor and offered burnt offerings and peace offerings. According to the account in 1 Chronicles, the Lord answered with fire from heaven on the altar of burnt offering, and the plague over Israel was stopped.

keyEvents.title: The Site of Solomon's Temple
keyEvents.description: Araunah's threshing floor was later chosen as the place where Solomon built the temple of the Lord in Jerusalem, giving this location lasting significance in Israel's history and worship.

versions.summary: Araunah (also known as Ornan) was a Jebusite who owned a threshing floor on Mount Moriah in Jerusalem. He is known for offering his threshing floor to King David free of charge to build an altar to the Lord, but David insisted on paying the full price. This threshing floor later became the site where Solomon's temple was built.
versions.title: The Jebusite Who Owned the Threshing Floor
versions.reason: [major] Araunah is not described as a 'leader' in the Bible. He was a Jebusite landowner/farmer who owned a threshing floor. Although some traditions suggest he may have been a Jebusite chieftain or king, his primary role in the text is that of a landowner. The role should be changed to something more precise.; [minor] The description mentions different amounts from 2 Samuel and Chronicles. It is worth clarifying that the difference likely arises because 2 Sam 24:24 refers to the purchase of the threshing floor itself and the oxen (50 shekels of silver), while 1 Chr 21:25 may refer to the purchase of the entire larger area (600 shekels of gold). The wording could be made slightly more nuanced.; [major] The profile lacks footnotes. There are several interesting historical, linguistic, and theological aspects regarding Araunah that deserve footnotes: the name variant Ornan, his Jebusite background, the price difference between 2 Samuel and 1 Chronicles, and the theological significance of the temple site.; [minor] The summary is good but could mention that the place is traditionally identified with Mount Moriah where Abraham nearly sacrificed Isaac (Gen 22), which provides a deeper theological context.

versions.summary: Araunah (also known as Ornan) was a Jebusite who owned a threshing floor on Mount Moriah in Jerusalem. When God sent a plague upon Israel as punishment for David's census, the angel of the Lord stopped at Araunah's threshing floor. The prophet Gad commanded David to build an altar there. Araunah offered King David his threshing floor, oxen, and tools free of charge, but David insisted on paying the full price, because he did not want to offer to the Lord something that cost him nothing. David built the altar and presented offerings, and the Lord stopped the plague. The place has deep theological significance: it is traditionally identified with Mount Moriah where Abraham was willing to sacrifice Isaac, and it later became the site where Solomon built the temple of the Lord.
versions.title: The Jebusite Who Owned the Threshing Floor
versions.reason: [minor] The summary is very similar to version 1 in structure and wording. Since this is the second version, the text should be rephrased more clearly to distinguish it from earlier attempts. Additionally, it can be strengthened theologically by highlighting the principle that genuine sacrifice costs something, as well as Araunah's generosity as a contrast.; [minor] The description states that 'the Lord answered with fire from heaven' – this detail is mentioned in 1 Chr 21:26, but not in 2 Sam 24:25. The description should clarify that this is according to the account in Chronicles, not both texts.; [minor] Araunah may have had a more prominent role among the Jebusites. Some scholars have suggested that the title 'Araunah' may have been a Jebusite royal title. The roles of 'local leader' or 'Jebusite chieftain' could be considered, but since this is uncertain, it might instead be mentioned in a footnote.; [minor] There is a missing footnote regarding the possible interpretation of 'Araunah' as a title rather than a personal name. Some scholars believe that the Jebusite word may mean 'lord' or 'prince', which could indicate that Araunah was a Jebusite leader or petty king.

footnotes.text: The name Araunah (Hebrew: אֲרַוְנָה) appears in various forms in biblical texts. In 2 Samuel he is called Araunah, while in 1 Chronicles he is called Ornan (Hebrew: אָרְנָן). The name variations may be due to different transcriptions of an originally non-Hebrew (Jebusite) name.

The Jebusites were the people who originally inhabited Jerusalem (also called Jebus) before David conquered the city around 1000 BC. The fact that Araunah still owned property in Jerusalem after the conquest suggests that David allowed the remaining Jebusites to live there in peace, possibly with certain rights.

The difference between the amounts in 2 Sam 24:24 (50 shekels of silver) and 1 Chr 21:25 (600 shekels of gold) has been widely discussed. A common explanation is that Samuel refers to the purchase of the threshing floor itself and the oxen, while Chronicles refers to the purchase of the entire larger area that later became the temple site.

The threshing floor on Mount Moriah holds deep theological significance in Jewish tradition. The place is identified with the Mount Moriah where Abraham was willing to sacrifice Isaac (Gen 22:2). That Solomon's temple was later built exactly here (2 Chr 3:1) creates a theological connection between Abraham's faith, David's offering, and the worship of the temple.

Archaeological excavations on the Temple Mount are extremely limited due to the site's religious sensitivity. It has therefore not been possible to identify traces of the original threshing floor archaeologically, but the bedrock beneath the Dome of the Rock is traditionally believed to mark the location.

In rabbinic tradition, Araunah's threshing floor is linked to the cosmological center—the 'navel' of the world (Even HaShetiyya, the Foundation Stone). According to the Talmud (Yoma 54b), this was the stone upon which the world was founded and which stood in the Holy of Holies in the temple.

Some scholars have suggested that 'Araunah' is not a personal name but a Jebusite title related to the Hurrian word 'ewri-ne', meaning 'lord' or 'prince'. If this is correct, Araunah may have been the last Jebusite king or chieftain in Jerusalem after David's conquest, who was allowed to retain his property as part of a peaceful transition.
